title: Vendor comparison field guide
summary: Practical field guide for SDRs, AEs and enablement to position Redwood against a set of popular LLM endpoint vendors. Focus is on short scripts, subtle traps customers fall into when evaluating hosted-only providers, and concrete counterplays for pricing, reliability, and compliance objections.
elevator_pitches: For engineers: "Redwood gives you the same simple REST SDK you expect while letting you move from hosted to dedicated to private without refactoring your stack—so you can optimize cost and latency as usage grows."
For platform leads: "We treat serving as a first-class product—predictable latency, per-route cost visibility, and rollout tools that let you manage risk across teams."
For procurement/security: "A single vendor that supports hosted APIs plus Private/VPC and compliant enterprise installs reduces integration risk and keeps audit trails centralized."
primary_win_themes: Unified runtime: no re-architect when migrating from hosted to dedicated/private
Operational transparency: token-level cost and latency visibility per model/route
Cost controls: intelligent batching + quantization guidance that moves the needle on unit economics
Reliability fallback patterns: automatic model/region fallbacks to protect SLAs
feature_comparisons:
Quick matrix (high level):

Provider             | Hosted API | Dedicated / Reserved | Private / VPC | Model Catalog & Profiling | Observability (per-route) | Rollouts & Fallbacks | Cost tooling
---------------------|------------|---------------------|---------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|--------------
Common hosted-only   | Yes        | No                  | No            | Limited                   | Basic                     | Manual               | None / simple
Hybrid vendors       | Yes        | Yes (some)          | Partial       | Medium                    | Per-model                 | Canary               | Partial
Redwood              | Yes        | Yes                 | Yes           | Curated + perf profiles  | Token-level, traceable    | Canary + auto-fallback | Batching, quantization advisor

Notes: matrix omits model family parity (customers often assume parity but attention to context length, KV cache behavior and quantization support matters).
hidden_traps_and_countermeasures: Trap: Price per token looks cheap in sandbox but cost balloons as usage shifts to long-context dialogs. Counter: Show a modeled bill for a sample workload using our batching and caching assumptions; highlight dedicated pricing options.

Trap: Vendor claims 'low latency' from single-region benchmarks. Counter: Ask for p95/p99 on real traffic patterns and show our multi-region fallback and durability story; bring SRE notes on cold-start and KV cache warmup behavior.

Trap: 'We can self-host later' — teams assume portability is easy. Counter: Walk through the code and infra changes needed to move from hosted to private on the competitor's stack vs Redwood’s consistent API surface and deployment abstraction.
Trap: Security checklist pass on paper but lack of auditability in practice. Counter: Request sample audit logs and demonstrate our KMS/HSM integrations + searchable audit trails in Console.

Trap: Model parity promises hide runtime differences (quantization, kernel selection). Counter: Recommend small perf/quality evals on representative prompts and show our model profiles and quantization guidance.
objection_handling_scripts: Objection: 'Your hosted price is higher than Vendor X.' \nScript: 'Totally fair — can we model a 6-month usage run? Most teams see hosted price parity once batching and prefix caching are applied; if predictability matters, our Dedicated plans often reduce unit cost and give you SLOs.'

Objection: 'We already have a cloud provider with managed endpoints.' \nScript: 'Many infra teams underestimate the integration/operational burden of maintaining inference pipelines across business units. Redwood surfaces per-route cost, tracing and rollouts so the central platform can enforce guardrails without slowing down product teams.'

Objection: 'We need air-gapped/on-prem — can you support that?' \nScript: 'Yes — our Private option includes on-prem deploys and a customer-managed control plane. We’ll scope network and KMS integration during POC so you can validate audit and data flows.'

Objection: 'Vendor Y has newer models.' \nScript: 'Model velocity is important; we curate widely used open models and publish perf profiles. More importantly, our runtime and routing let you fall back to lower-cost variants without changing your application code.'
deal_stages_and_play_actions: Discovery: Identify if evaluation is latency, cost, or compliance-first. If compliance: request copy of security questionnaire early.
POC scoping: Propose a small guided POC with a 2-week traffic replay and our cost/latency report; include model evaluation on customer's prompt set.
Negotiation: Offer a dedicated capacity baseline + a usage runway to prevent sticker shock. Use historical run-rate modeling to justify reserved commit levels.
Close: Align on rollout plan (canary, A/B, auto-fallback), success metrics (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens), and audit log retention.
competitive_signals_to_watch: Provider announces free credits for developers — watch for volume-driven lock-in attempts.
New pricing tiers with hidden egress or storage fees — ask for an example invoice.
Announcements about proprietary model exclusivity — surface as a feature / lock-in risk to customers.
Provider marketing uses single-benchmark latency claims without p99 or sustained throughput numbers.
suggested_next_steps: Turn this doc into a 1-pager cheat sheet for SDRs (top 3 scripts + 2 short choke points).
Create a POC template: traffic replay, cost model, and 7-day perf report for field eng to run with prospects.
Add a small eval kit to the console that auto-runs customer prompts against candidate models and produces a quality vs cost summary.
